facts.fact: Farkas North American White young adult SDs as reproduced in a face-recognition paper (secondary citation of Farkas Table 0.3, not verified against the book): ex-ex SD 3.6 mm (males), 4 mm (females); n-gn height SD 6.8 mm (males), 5.2 mm (females). Means not given in the excerpt.
Farkas's full adult means and SDs could not be retrieved from the search results; the primary source is Farkas, Anthropometry of the Head and Face (Raven Press, New York, 1994).

The Farkas craniofacial norms are based on direct anthropometry with N=2326 subjects, described as North American White adults and children; the 3D Facial Norms (3DFN) comparison dataset is N=2454 collected by stereophotogrammetry.
The 3DFN database contains 2454 participants aged 3-40 years (952 male, 1502 female); it is cross-sectional with each person appearing once.

3DFN summary-level phenotypic data (landmarks, anthropometric measurements, demographics) are non-controlled and openly downloadable from facebase.org; individual-level data require a Data Access Request reviewed by the FaceBase Data Access Committee.
The 3DFN resource includes sex-specific 3D growth curves and a MATLAB toolbox for assessing individuals against the models.
The 3DFN paper reports 34 inter-landmark measurements and defines landmarks such as en, al, ch; the snippet did not include adult mouth-width values.
Kolar (1993) criticized the Farkas dataset, with the most serious problems attributed to inconsistent data-collection protocols; the original Kolar paper was not retrieved.
Traditional anthropometry norm datasets are confined to narrow age ranges and share demographic limitations, per the 3DFN description.

A 2019 comparison (Weinberg et al.) found considerable differences between 3DFN and Farkas norms; the authors attribute discrepancies partly to measurement method, possibly secular trends and ethnic composition.
Direct vs 3D photogrammetry agreement in a systematic review (Weinberg et al.): most differences below 2 mm despite some statistically significant differences.
Direct measurement vs photogrammetry: highest mean difference 0.30 mm; direct vs 3D stereophotogrammetry: 0.21 mm (figures from a search snippet; the source study was not opened).
CT-derived measurement for Go-Go was 2.34 mm larger than the 3dMD stereophotogrammetry value in one study, showing modality-dependent offsets.
Kosovo-Albanian adults (Staka et al. 2017): male morphological facial height (n-gn) SD 6.366 mm; female SD 5.004 mm; male n-gn mean 125.82 mm, female 115.53 mm (means from search snippet).
Kosovo-Albanian adults: intercanthal width (en-en) male mean 32.49 mm (SD 2.59), female 31.78 mm (SD 2.25); sex difference t=2.078, p=0.039.
Indian medical students (n=200; 104 male, 96 female; BHU Uttar Pradesh): morphological facial height male 121.64 ± 6.47 mm, female 113.63 ± 4.61 mm.
Facial asymmetry study (n=297 adults aged 19-42; 147 women, 150 men): right alare-midline mean 17.34 mm (male) vs 15.39 mm (female); males larger on all reported landmarks.

Southern-Spain European adults with normal occlusion (3D): mouth-to-intercanthal width ratio about 1.59 (men) and 1.52 (women); intercanthal-to-nasal width ratio 0.89 (men) and 1.01 (women); nasal mean difference reported 5.23 mm.

3D normotypes paper (2025-era, maxillofacial planning): intercanthal width en_r-en_l ranges 20-41 mm in one group and 21-39 mm in another; a sex table lists 37.0 and 28.9 mm; sex and population labels not confirmed from the snippet. Ranges are computed as mean ± 2 SD (about 95% of the reference population).
Hong Kong Chinese young adults (3D): intercanthal width male mean 40.61 mm, female 38.27 mm; males significantly larger.

Malay adults (3D stereophotogrammetry): intercanthal width 35.74 mm (men) and 35.03 mm (women); nose width 39.59 mm (men) and 36.67 mm (women); nose width definition should be checked as it is larger than typical alar width values.

Systematic review of inter-ethnic variability (Fang, Clapham, Chung 2011, Plast Reconstr Surg): pooled 11 neoclassical linear facial measurements from 2,359 men and women across 27 ethnic groups; coefficient of variation used; forehead height showed the largest inter-ethnic variation in facial proportions.
Wen et al. (2015) Bayesian meta-analysis of photogrammetric inter-ethnic facial variation is a separate work from the 2011 systematic review and should not be conflated with it.
No 2025-2026 adult normative table reporting nasal width, mouth width and intercanthal width together from 3D landmarks was found in the search results.
Search for Headspace as a 3D facial norms source returned no results; it could not be confirmed as a norms source.

contradictions: Intercanthal (en-en) adult means disagree across populations: Kosovo-Albanian males 32.49 mm and females 31.78 mm; Malay 35.74/35.03 mm; Hong Kong Chinese 40.61/38.27 mm; normotype paper 37.0 and 28.9 mm (labels unclear). Likely due to landmark definitions (en-en vs biocular), modality (caliper vs 3D) and population; they are not directly comparable.
Nose width in the Malay 3D study (39.59 mm males) is much larger than typical alar width values, suggesting a different landmark definition than alar width; comparisons need definition matching.

Direct-vs-3D agreement is reported as sub-2 mm for most measures (systematic review), yet the 3DFN vs Farkas comparison found considerable differences; discrepancies appear to be method, time and population dependent.
Farkas SDs quoted in a 2023 face-recognition paper (ex-ex 3.6/4 mm; n-gn 6.8/5.2 mm) could not be checked against the primary book.
